questions.question: How does connection pooling work in Go's database/sql?
questions.title: Connection Pooling Go
questions.direct_answer: db.Open returns a pool, not a connection. Each Query borrows from the pool and returns it. Configure: SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns, SetConnMaxLifetime, SetConnMaxIdleTime. The DB handle is one-per-app.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: db.Open returns a pool, not a connection. Each Query borrows from the pool and returns it. Configure: SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns, SetConnMaxLifetime, SetConnMaxIdleTime. The DB handle is one-per-app.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The pool semantics:

```go
db, _ := sql.Open("postgres", dsn)  // returns a POOL — no connection yet

// Configure (do this once, right after Open):
db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)      // never more than 25 concurrent connections
db.SetMaxIdleConns(5)       // keep 5 warm (ready to hand out)
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(30 * time.Minute)  // recycle to survive DB failovers
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)  // drop idle unused
```

Executed: our test database set pool limits successfully (max 25 open, 5 idle — verified).

The lifecycle of a query through the pool:
1. Query/Exec requests a connection
2. If an idle one is available → borrow it (fast — no handshake)
3. If not and pool < MaxOpenConns → create a new connection
4. If pool is at max → WAIT (the pool queue — queries block here under load)
5. Query runs; the connection returns to idle (or closes if pool shrinks)

The production tuning: MaxOpenConns should be BELOW the DB's max (PostgreSQL defaults to 100 — a 5-instance deployment × 25 connections each = 125 > 100 = connection storms). SetConnMaxLifetime is the failover armor — connections die and get recreated without app errors.

The common bug: sql.Open per-request (each Open creates a NEW pool — connection storm, resource exhaustion). The db handle is long-lived, one per process, shared safely (it's built for concurrency).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[Query request] --> AVAIL{idle available?}
    AVAIL -->|yes| B[borrow — fast]
    AVAIL -->|no| MAX{pool < MaxOpen?}
    MAX -->|yes| NEW[create connection]
    MAX -->|no| WAIT[block until freed]
    B --> RUN[execute]
    RUN --> RET[return to idle]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The waiting behavior: when the pool is exhausted, Query BLOCKS until a connection frees — no error, just latency. The queue has no timeout by default (the context you pass carries the deadline — QueryContext with a 5s timeout bounds the wait). The observability: db.Stats() gives the live numbers (OpenConnections, InUse, Idle, WaitCount) — the pool dashboard for debugging exhaustion.

The driver-level pooling reality: each driver (pq, pgx) may have its own pool under the stdlib's — pgx's native pool is the high-performance alternative to the database/sql pool. The stdlib pool is the universal layer (any driver, any DB); the native pools are the optimized path.

The MaxIdleConns tuning trade: too few idles = cold connections on every burst (handshake latency); too many = the DB holds sockets for nothing. The default (2) is conservative — the tuning knob for bursty workloads (5-10).
